newsitem.title: USA: Clinton may intercede if tobacco talks stall - WSJ.
newsitem.headline: Clinton may intercede if tobacco talks stall - WSJ.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton urged negotiators in tobacco-settlement talks to keep pursuing an agreement, but would not preclude getting involved personally if he believes hopes of reaching a deal have been exhausted, the Wall Street Journal said in Thursday's electronic edition.
Clinton also told the Journal in an interview that he did not yet want to take a public stance on the dispute over whether cigarette makers should be given immunity from punitive damages.
The president said he wants negotiators to remain at the table to try to hammer out a deal before he would consider interceding.

"I don't want to rule in or out what I might say, but I want these parties to come to me and say, 'This is where we are. We've done all we can do, here's where we are,'" he said. "And I want them to do the very best they can first."

He added later, "They need to stay there, keep working, and try to resolve this thing and bring us all something which we can evaluate. Then, if I think it should be modified in some way, I could tell them I thought it should be modified."
The settlement talks have reached a fevered pitch in recent days as negotiators remain huddled in Washington in late-night sessions.
Forty states have sued the industry to recover Medicaid costs of treating smokers.
The White House has been monitoring the talks and any settlement would need approval from Clinton and Congress before it could be implemented.
